entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @hesmashena

The second issue of the specialized quarterly of the Payab Think Tank has been published.

🔴The Payab Quarterly, produced by the Payab Think Tank, aims to publish the opinions and initiatives of scholars in the fields of foreign policy, international relations, policymaking, and governance, following the style of journals based on policy reports.

🔷The editorial of this issue of the Payab Quarterly, titled "Political Psychology and International Relations," was written by Dr. Abbas Maleki, editor-in-chief of the Payab journal.

🔻This quarterly also features articles and notes including "The New Architecture of Strategic Relations with China and Russia: Authenticity and Comprehensive Capacity" by Dr. Mohammad Javad Zarif, "Sitting in Falsehood; or Wandering in the Wilderness? In Defense of Peaceful Nuclear Technology and a Third Way for Iran's National Security" by Dr. Hesamoddin Ashena, "Policymaking in Implementation; Rethinking Governance, Investment, and the Development of Iran's Oil and Gas Industry" by Dr. Gholamreza Manouchehri, "The Strait of Hormuz and the Dispute over Iranian Management" by Dr. Kourosh Ahmadi, "Foreign Policy and the Harmful Cycle of Decision-Making Expectation in Crisis Conditions" by Dr. Sasan Karimi, and "The Delegated and Unpredictable Iranian" by Dr. Seyed Jafar Hashemi.

🔻In the policy reports section, works have been published by Dr. Kiumars Ashtarian titled "The Right to Geography," Dr. Omid Asghari titled "Southophobia, the Right to Development, and Global Governance," Dr. Shafaei and Dr. Tabatabainejad titled "From the Strategy of Resistance to the Architecture of a New Order: The Question of Sustainable National Security," Dr. Mohammad Fekri titled "Opportunities and Risks of Post-War Street Gatherings," and Dr. Mohsen Shalbaf titled "The Rise of the Green Superpower; How Did China Surpass Europe and America in the Transition to Clean Technologies?"

🔻Further in the second issue of the Payab Quarterly, works by Amin Hasani, Amirparsa Garmsiri, Kasra Ghafouri, Mahya Danesh, Fatemeh Sadeghi Sheikh, and Ali Faryadras are also featured.

♦️The specialized Payab Quarterly, at 162 pages, is available for access and use by all interested parties on the Payab Think Tank website at www.paiab.org

entry.title: [hesmashena] I suspect it is precisely at this point that the headline can outrun the text.…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @hesmashena

I suspect it is precisely at this point that the headline can outrun the text. The core message is not necessarily that Iran is more powerful than America, China, or any other power. The core message is that Iran today, in the narrative being presented, is not an Iran that can be dragged back to its former position of dependency. This is no small distinction. In the text, three temporal planes are woven together: a past that must not return, a present that must be defended, and a future that must be more powerful than the present. That is why the message does not conclude in the past either; it moves toward the future. But it is precisely here that the most difficult question begins. "We will not go back" is not merely a statement about a foreign enemy. Not going back cannot be measured solely by missile range, the distance of enemy warships, or military operational capacity. If we take the concept of power seriously, then the economy, knowledge, technology, the quality of governance, public trust, human capital, social cohesion, and the ability to solve problems are all part of that same arena. A country that does not want to go back must be able to simultaneously withstand external threats and, on the domestic front, create the capacity for a better life, greater hope, and the possibility of broader progress. This is where the narrative of power meets people's everyday experience. The narrower the gap between the two, the more the phrase "we will not go back" transforms from a political slogan into a collective experience. The wider this gap grows, the less the foreign enemy even needs to challenge the narrative; people's daily lives will do it for them. The recent message can be read from various angles. One can debate its claim to power, the Strait of Hormuz, regional resistance, or its religious symbolism. But the thread binding all these elements together is, to my mind, too clear to be lost in noisy headlines: "The enemy wants Iran to return to the past; the text says that past is over." The question of Iran's future lies in exactly the same place: let us not go back — not only in independence and security, but in every component that truly makes a nation powerful.
